t: Introduction: topic, aim and plan
n: In this lecture we study the ethical aspects of dying and death. Chapter XI considers the ethical aspects of dying and death, the question of “brain death” and its significance in modern medical practice. The plan is as follows: dying and death, clinical and biological death, brain death, the Declaration of Sydney of the World Medical Association, that is, the WMA. At the end the vegetative state is considered: the permanent, that is, persistent vegetative state, PVS for short, is one of the difficult problems of resuscitation science. The basic concepts: dying, or the terminal period, clinical death, biological death, brain death and the vegetative state.

t: Death is a philosophical and ethical problem
n: Death is a philosophical and ethical problem. Death has always been mysterious to people and has to a certain extent aroused fear. Every event that begins has a natural, logical end, and human life is no exception. The problem of death is one of the main questions of the philosophical, ethical-religious and biomedical view of life. A person's attitude to death forms a whole system of ethical interconnections and dependencies.

t: Death and dying: the difference
n: First let us distinguish death and dying. Death is recognised as an accomplished fact, whereas dying is a process lasting for varying lengths of time. The fact of death can be recorded, while dying stretches from seconds to months, in some cases up to 10 to 15 years. The process of dying is called the terminal, that is, the borderline period. Remember: dying and death are not the same thing. Do not confuse the process with the final fact.

t: Duration of the terminal (borderline) period
n: The duration of the terminal, that is, borderline period varies. Death is an accomplished fact, while dying is a process lasting for varying lengths of time. The most rapid dying is measured in seconds. In slower dying this period stretches to days and months. The specialist literature gives cases in which the period of dying with medical care was stretched to 10 to 15 years. So the terminal period varies over a very wide range.

t: The formation of resuscitation science
n: Now on the formation of resuscitation science. Until the middle of the last century, arrest of circulation and respiration was assessed as an irreversible state. The distinction between clinical and biological death played the main role in the formation of a new science, resuscitation science. Resuscitation science studies the mechanisms of dying and the questions of returning a dying organism to life. This science was able to overcome arrest of circulation and respiration, previously regarded as a reliable criterion of death.

t: Clinical death: between life and death
n: Clinical death is an intermediate state of the organism between life and death. The heart and breathing stop, while the higher parts of the brain work for 5 to 6 minutes. During this period the possibility of returning the organism to life is preserved. If recovery does not occur, biological death takes place. In conditions of hypothermia the period of clinical death may be longer. From the standpoint of law and ethics this is not death, since the possibility of return is preserved.

t: Emergency help in clinical death: the ethical requirement
n: Let us pay attention to the question of emergency help in clinical death. Clinical death is an intermediate state between life and death. After the heart and breathing stop, the higher parts of the brain work for a short time, that is, 5 to 6 minutes. From the legal and ethical standpoint clinical death cannot be assessed as death, since during this period the possibility of returning the organism to life is preserved. Therefore the ethical approach requires the medical worker to give emergency medical help in clinical death. In some patients the help removes the threat of death. Sometimes, however, it only prolongs dying and creates an ethical problem.

t: Clinical and biological death: a comparison
n: Let us compare clinical and biological death. In clinical death the heart and breathing have stopped, the higher parts of the brain work for 5 to 6 minutes, and the possibility of return is preserved. If the heart and breathing are not restored, irreversible changes begin in the brain and biological death occurs. In biological death the physiological processes in cells and tissues cease irreversibly, and there is no possibility of return. Attention: clinical death differs from biological death. In hypothermia the period of clinical death may be longer.

t: Quick question 1
n: The first quick question. What is the terminal period? It is the process of dying; it may last from seconds to days, weeks and months. How long do the higher parts of the brain work in clinical death? About 5 to 6 minutes. Why can clinical death not be regarded as death? Because the possibility of returning to life is preserved. What is the essence of biological death? The irreversible cessation of physiological processes in cells and tissues.

t: Case analysis 1: help in clinical death
n: The first case analysis is help in clinical death. The situation: the patient's heartbeat and breathing have stopped. The higher parts of the brain are still working for a short time, that is, 5 to 6 minutes. Question: is the physician obliged to give help? Yes. The ethical approach requires emergency medical help in clinical death. This state cannot be regarded as death, since the possibility of returning the organism to life is preserved. In hypothermia this period may be longer. Attention: if the heart and breathing are not restored, irreversible changes begin and biological death occurs.

t: The problem of brain death: sensitivity of tissues
n: Now we turn to the problem of brain death, and first of all look at the sensitivity of tissues. The phylogenetic age of tissues differs; young tissues are more sensitive to influence. Nervous tissue is more sensitive than muscle and bone tissue. The most sensitive structure is the cerebral cortex, the least sensitive is the peripheral nerve. The order of sensitivity in descending order is as follows: the cerebral cortex, subcortical structures, the brainstem, the spinal cord, the peripheral nerve.

t: Tissues do not die at the same time: supravital reactions
n: Tissues do not die at the same time. Irreversible changes are observed first of all in the cortex, and the integrative activity of the central nervous system is disturbed. Even when an irreversible change has occurred in the cortex, that is, “brain death”, the other organs have not yet died. Therefore in the corpse, in the first hours, some tissues respond to mechanical, electrical and chemical influence. These are supravital reactions. After brain death the heart and kidneys remain alive for 15 to 20 minutes at most, the cornea for 6 to 8 hours. Transplantation is based on this.

t: Personal status and the brain
n: Personal status is linked with the brain. The status of a human being as a person is directly linked with the activity of the brain, mainly of the cerebral cortex. When the brain dies, the human being loses his personality and individuality. In the 1960s and 70s, thanks to advances in resuscitation science, the former criterion, that is, circulation and respiration, became insufficient; the criterion of brain death appeared. Attention: a heartbeat does not mean that the person is alive. Under the concept of brain death a human being is regarded as dead even if the heart is working.

t: Death of the individual and death of cells
n: Now we dwell on the terms for death. W. Durwald (1981) called brain death “individual death”. He called the death of the remaining tissues and organs “cell death”. Now the death of the cortex is also called by the terms “death of the individual” and “death of the person”. That is, the death of the cerebral cortex is called the death of the person, and another name for the death of this cortex is the death of the individual.

t: Survival time of organs after brain death
n: After brain death the organs do not die at the same time. Some organs keep signs of life for a relatively short time and then die. In the heart and kidneys this period is up to 15 to 20 minutes, in the cornea of the eye 6 to 8 hours. In other tissues this period may reach several hours. The removal of organs and tissues from a corpse for transplantation is based precisely on this feature.

t: Yudin: the “zone of uncertainty, vagueness”
n: In Yudin's view, patients in coma stand in a “zone of uncertainty, vagueness” between the concepts “definitely alive” and “definitely dead”. Physicians express this state thus: the person is still alive but unconscious; one must await his physical death from such factors as hunger and infection. For citizens it is rather difficult to accept the recording of the death of a person whose heart is beating and who is breathing on the basis of brain death. This state gives rise to various misunderstandings and ethical problems.

t: Three views of death
n: There are three views of death. In medicine clinical and biological death are distinguished; the main sign of biological death is brain death. In the religious understanding the physical body is doomed to perish and the soul is immortal; death is not the end of life but its continuation in another form. The third position rests on psychophysiological study of brain activity and transpersonal psychology; the experiences of clinical death are analysed. The task of bioethics is to study the phenomenon of death as a biosocial system that has entered the socio-cultural relations of society.

t: Quick question 2
n: The second quick question. First question: what are supravital reactions? They are the response of certain tissues in the corpse, in the first hours after death, to mechanical, electrical and chemical influence. Second question: why are they observed? Even after the irreversible death of the cerebral cortex, some tissues keep vital properties for a time. Third question: what is personal status linked with? Directly with the activity of the brain, mainly of the cerebral cortex. Fourth question: what is cell death? According to W. Durwald, brain death is “individual death”, and the death of the remaining tissues and organs is “cell death”.

t: Case analysis 2: an unconscious patient with a beating heart
n: The second case analysis. The situation: in a patient with a beating heart, on artificial ventilation, brain activity has ceased completely and irreversibly. His relatives consider him alive. Question: why is it hard for relatives to accept death? Because the concept of brain death does not accord with traditional ideas of death, and even contradicts them. Analysis: the fact of death must be recorded by a consilium of experienced specialists using modern clinical and paraclinical methods. Attention: a heartbeat does not indicate a living person. In brain death the person is regarded as dead even if cardiac activity is preserved.

t: The reply of Pope Pius XII (1957)
n: Now on the reply of Pope Pius XII. The development of technology for artificially maintaining life created problems in determining the fact of death. In 1957 the international congress of anaesthesiologists and resuscitation specialists appealed to Pope Pius XII with a request to clarify the criteria. The Pope replied: determining the fact of death is a matter not for the Church but for physicians. The Church approved this. So determining the fact of death was recognised as the physician's competence.

t: The term and definition of brain death
n: We become acquainted with the term and definition of brain death. The term “brain death” was first used by French scientists to describe very deep coma. By Gurvich's definition (1997), it is the death of the brain: spontaneous breathing ceases, reflexes fade, unconsciousness is irreversible. Irreversible changes in the central nervous system necessary for life, if not restored by treatment or artificial systems, are accepted as the death of the person. The concept is scientifically grounded: an irreversible change in the brain is equated with the death of the human being as a person and individual.

t: Brain death and the traditional idea: a contradiction
n: Brain death contradicts the traditional idea. The concept of brain death does not accord with traditional ideas of death and, in a certain sense, contradicts them. The traditional criterion is the stopping of the heart and breathing, and if the heart beats the person is regarded as alive. In brain death the criterion is the irreversible cessation of brain function; cardiac activity may be preserved, while the person is regarded as dead. This is so even if the heart and other signs of life are preserved. Therefore recording the fact is complex: it must be carried out by a consilium of experienced specialists.

t: The Harvard criteria (1968)
n: The Harvard criteria were developed in 1968. They were drawn up by a group of specialists in the USA. The criteria are based on brain death and are intended for determining the death of a human being. The main aim is to eliminate useless resuscitation measures and expenditure of resources. The chronology is as follows: in 1968 the Harvard criteria; in the same year the Declaration of Sinai of the WMA adopted the criteria of brain death, and in 1983 the declaration was supplemented.

t: The WMA Declaration of Sinai: content
n: Let us dwell on the content of the WMA Declaration of Sinai. The WMA declaration was adopted in 1968 and supplemented in 1983. In the source it is called the “Declaration of Sydney”. The declaration states that modern trends in medicine, in particular the development of transplantology, require a new approach to recording the fact of death. The task of the attending physician is to preserve not individual cells but the integrity of the person. Therefore what matters is to determine not the death of individual cells but the moment when, despite resuscitation, the integrity of the organism is irreversibly broken.

t: The Declaration of Sinai: time of death and requirements
n: The Declaration of Sinai defines the time of death and the requirements. The time of death is the time of irreversible cessation of the integrative functions of the brain, including the brainstem. The steps are as follows: the integrative function of the brain ceases, the brainstem ceases too, and this time is regarded as the time of death. At this time resuscitation may be stopped and, in cases permitted by law, an organ may be removed. If an organ is to be removed, death is confirmed by at least two physicians who are not directly interested.

t: Islamic bioethics and brain death
n: In Islamic bioethics the attitude to brain death varies. Muslim jurists considered complete cessation of the heartbeat a sufficient criterion for declaring a person dead. The concept of brain death in Muslim society is a neologism; the problem arose when the brainstem was able to maintain a vital function with the help of respiration. IOMS, at its symposia in 1985 and 1996, recognised brain death as an acceptable criterion of death. In 1995 in Iran, on the basis of the principle of non-maleficence, adoption of the criteria of brain death was rejected; the opinions of the fiqh academies differ.

t: Requirements for criteria of determining the time of death
n: The criteria for determining the time of death must, ethically and legally, meet four requirements. The first requirement is a scientific basis: it must be reliably possible to distinguish whom it is possible to save and whom it is not. The second is practical convenience. The third is objectivity: any qualified specialist applies the criterion in the same way, and its correctness can be checked. The fourth is conformity with the norms of society.

t: Clinical signs of brain death
n: Now the clinical signs of brain death. They are divided into four groups. The first group is consciousness: unconsciousness is complete and persistent. The second is respiration and muscles: there is no spontaneous breathing, and muscle atony is observed. The third is response reactions: there is no response to pain and light. The fourth is reflexes: the corneal, pharyngeal and tracheal reflexes are absent. Attention: before the diagnosis is made, causes such as drugs, poisoning and hypothermia must be excluded.

t: Quick question 3
n: The third quick question. First question: when and for what purpose were the Harvard criteria developed? Answer: in 1968, USA; to eliminate useless resuscitation. Second question: when, according to the Declaration of Sinai, is the time of death? When the integrative functions of the brain, including the function of the brainstem, have irreversibly ceased. Third question: who records death if an organ is to be removed? At least two physicians who are not directly interested. Fourth question: name at least three clinical signs of brain death. Absence of breathing, atony, absence of pupillary and pain response, and so on.

t: Case analysis 3: the commission confirming death
n: The third case analysis is the commission confirming death. The situation: a patient with suspected brain death is in intensive care, and it is planned to remove an organ from the corpse for transplantation. Question: who forms the commission? The commission must include an anaesthesiologist-resuscitation specialist and a neurologist. Specialists engaged in organ removal and transplantation are not included. According to the Declaration of Sydney, if an organ is to be removed, death is confirmed by at least two physicians who are not directly interested. Attention: a transplant specialist cannot be the physician confirming death. These two functions must not be mixed in one person.

t: Reliability of the diagnosis of brain death
n: The reliability of the diagnosis of brain death is a central ethical question. The concept of brain death was developed in neurology independently of the needs of transplantology. The reliability of the diagnosis falls almost entirely within the professional competence of neurologists. The organisational and financial independence of the diagnosing institutions from transplant specialists is the most important principle ensuring trust. There are three procedures for obtaining organs: routine inquiry, presumed consent and presumed refusal. Informing the population about these procedures is also a basic condition of trust.

t: Diagnosis of brain death: conditions and commission (RF, 1993)
n: The conditions and commission for diagnosing brain death are considered under the RF instruction of 1993. First the cause is established; factors such as drugs, poisoning, shock and hypothermia are excluded. The chain is as follows: the cause and mechanism are determined, excluding conditions are checked, the commission gives its conclusion, the record is approved and resuscitation is stopped. The commission members have at least 5 years' experience; the commission includes an anaesthesiologist-resuscitation specialist and a neurologist. This instruction is not applied to determine brain death in children.

t: Cadaveric donation: conditions in Arab-Islamic countries
n: For cadaveric donation, conditions have also been laid down in Arab-Islamic countries. The Council of Health Ministers of the Arab-Islamic countries adopted a draft law on human organ transplantation of 11 articles. With the consent of the deceased's relatives, if he did not object during his life, organ transplantation is possible. Death is determined by three specialist physicians, including a neurologist; the surgeon who performs the operation must not be in this group. The sale and purchase of an organ, or giving it as a gift for reward, is prohibited; the operation takes place in recognised medical centres.

t: Uzbek legislation and examination of the corpse
n: We turn to Uzbek legislation and the question of examining the corpse. In foreign experience this procedure is mainly developed by anaesthesiologist-resuscitation specialists and neurologists. The absence of clear criteria creates serious difficulties in the physician's work. Under Article 40 of the law, the procedure for recording is set by the Ministry. Order No. 153 (2012) lays down the rules of forensic medical examination of the corpse. Recording brain death in the established manner is linked with the beginning of the examination of the corpse. Before the first changes appear, that is, cooling, lividity and rigidity of the corpse, the fact of death is recorded first.

t: The vegetative state: definition
n: Now the definition of the vegetative state. The vegetative state, from the Latin for “plant-like”, is the biological rhythm of life of an organism in an unconscious state because of the cessation of brain activity. In this state brain death has not occurred, but there is practically no possibility of restoring consciousness. Attention: the vegetative state differs from brain death. Medical help preserves only biological life by maintaining the basic vital functions, that is, parenteral feeding and care. Such a life usually cannot be the life of an independent, separate individual; processes of degradation, that is, decline, intensify with time.

t: Signs of the persistent vegetative state (PVS)
n: Signs of the persistent vegetative state, that is, PVS. A vegetative state that continues for a long time is called persistent, that is, a lasting vegetative state, PVS for short. The first sign is complete unconsciousness: the patient is unaware of himself and those around him. The second is alternating periods of sleep and wakefulness. The third is that vegetative functions are preserved. Attention: in PVS the brainstem functions are preserved, whereas in brain death the brainstem also dies.

t: PVS: causes, prevalence and social problem
n: On the causes, prevalence and social problem of PVS. PVS may arise after comas of various origins, brain injuries and neurological diseases. According to various authors, in countries of the world there are 2 to 13 cases of PVS per 100 000 population. Such patients require long treatment and large expenditure, so PVS is a serious problem for the healthcare system. An example: according to media reports, S. Vyazemsky, a former soloist of “Freestyle”, after being resuscitated in 2015, remained in a vegetative state until his death in 2020.

t: Prognosis in PVS and the 1989 WMA statement
n: In PVS the recovery of consciousness is uncertain, and medicine cannot give an exact prognosis. As time passes, the probability of recovering consciousness falls; full recovery is regarded as casuistry. The WMA, that is, the World Medical Association, adopted a statement on PVS in 1989. In it the time limits are as follows: if it continues for several weeks, a vegetative state; as a general rule 12 months, and in persons over 50, 6 months. After that a decision is made to continue or to stop.

t: Case analysis 4: PVS and decision-making
n: The fourth case analysis is about PVS and decision-making. The situation: according to a media report, the former soloist of “Freestyle” was resuscitated in 2015 after coronary death and remained in a vegetative state until his death. Question: how is preserving or ending life approached in a patient with prolonged PVS? After the time limits, the decision is made by the physician in accordance with law and ethics. Attention: PVS is not brain death. In PVS brain death has not occurred, but there is practically no possibility of restoring consciousness. Patients with PVS require long treatment and large funds; this is a serious problem for healthcare.

t: Conclusion and review questions
n: Let us conclude. The terminal period is the process of dying, stretching from seconds to months. Clinical death is reversible, biological death irreversible. Brain death is irreversible unconsciousness with loss of spontaneous breathing and reflexes. The Declaration of Sydney, that is, of Sinai (1968; supplemented in 1983), recognised it as a criterion. PVS is unconsciousness, but the sleep–wake cycle is preserved. WMA 1989: several weeks, PVS; 12 months, or 6 months in persons over 50, the criterion of irreversibility. For self-testing, review: the terminal period; the difference between clinical and biological death; the zone of uncertainty; the content of the Declaration of Sydney; the criteria of death; the signs of PVS; the WMA recommendations.
